AGR: Agentic Generative Retrieval with Tool-Augmented Search

Ming Yang Affiliation: Fudan University    Yaqi Yin Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology    Zhibo Wang Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology    Xiaoze Jiang Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology    Jingwei Zhuo Affiliation: Unaffiliated    Chao Zhang, Quanzhi Zhu, Weiguo Zheng, Liang Zeng, Yunfeng Zhao, Affiliation: Fudan University Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology    Jiaqiang Liu, Kefeng Wang, Yupeng Huang, Kaiqiao Zhan, Xuanping Li Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology
Abstract

Large-scale search and recommendation systems derive much of their retrieval quality from rich, heterogeneous features, yet existing generative retrieval (GR) methods struggle to exploit such feature ecosystems efficiently. Static feature injection either encodes all available signals or places them according to predetermined schemes, increasing serving cost and introducing irrelevant or conflicting evidence. More fundamentally, existing methods cannot adaptively determine when a feature is needed, which feature to select, or where it should influence hierarchical Semantic ID (SID) generation. We propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), a tool-augmented paradigm that interleaves SID generation with on-demand feature acquisition. Conditioned on the request and decoded SID prefix, AGR decides whether to invoke a tool, which feature to acquire, and where its observation should influence subsequent decoding, thereby steering generation toward feature-consistent SID branches. To supervise this behavior, we construct tool-augmented trajectories based on feature applicability and information gain along the SID hierarchy, and train the model through SID pretraining followed by tool-augmented fine-tuning. Experiments on an industrial dataset and three public benchmarks, together with an online A/B test, consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of AGR.

1 Introduction

Generative Retrieval (GR) casts retrieval as autoregressive identifier generation (Tay et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Bevilacqua et al., 2022). Following TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023), items are commonly represented by hierarchical Semantic IDs (SIDs) learned through residual quantization. This paradigm has also been successfully adopted in large-scale industrial scenarios (Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025c; Team et al., 2026).

Deploying GR in industrial systems, however, exposes a fundamental mismatch between request-conditioned SID generation and the feature-intensive nature of such systems (Zhai et al., 2024). Large-scale retrieval depends heavily on heterogeneous signals, such as user profiles, behavioral histories, and freshness cues (Hou et al., 2026). Yet existing GR methods scale poorly with the number of features (Figure 1), typically appending all signals to the input or injecting them according to a predetermined scheme, making it difficult to jointly maintain retrieval quality and serving efficiency (Zhou et al., 2026). Specifically, encoding all features indiscriminately inflates serving cost and introduces irrelevant or conflicting evidence, as feature utility is inherently request-dependent: a feature indispensable for one request may be pure noise for another (Zhang et al., 2026a). This raises the question of when a feature should be incorporated. Meanwhile, injecting features at a fixed scheme cannot adapt to the decoding state, but residual quantization induces a hierarchical SID space where different depths resolve distinctions at different granularities. Therefore, a feature highly informative at one level may be irrelevant at others. This raises the question of where a feature should influence generation. Addressing both questions is crucial for efficient and scalable GR deployment in industrial search, yet effective feature injection remains largely overlooked.

To this end, we propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), which reformulates generative retrieval as an interleaved process of SID generation and feature acquisition. AGR encapsulates heterogeneous features as tools, each uniquely identified by a tool token. Conditioned on the current decoding state, the model decides whether to emit a tool token and, if so, which tool to invoke. The acquired feature values are then represented as observation tokens that reshape the probability distribution over subsequent SID tokens, steering generation toward feature-consistent paths. As features are introduced only when the decoding state warrants them, AGR reduces feature noise and naturally aligns feature granularity with the coarse-to-fine progression of SID generation. Through this adaptive tool use, AGR shifts generative retrieval from passive SID generation to agentic decision-making over both items and features.

Contributions. Our contributions are shown as follows:

  • •

    Driven by the industrial need to exploit rich, heterogeneous feature ecosystems in GR, we systematically reveal and quantify two fundamental limitations of static feature injection in GR: it is neither request-adaptive (when to inject) nor level-adaptive (where to inject). We further argue that features should be acquired on demand and injected at the right SID depth.

  • •

    We propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), which encapsulates feature injection as tool invocation and thereby unifies adaptive feature selection with dynamic placement into a single decoding process, paving the way for exploiting rich features in real-world retrieval systems.

  • •

    We derive principled criteria for choosing which tool to invoke and where it is most informative along the SID hierarchy, so that each tool call steers decoding toward feature-consistent branches, and instantiate them in a two-stage pipeline of SID pretraining and tool-augmented fine-tuning.

  • •

    We evaluate AGR on Kuaishou Search system and three widely used public benchmarks. AGR improves recall by up to +14.04% over baseline and yields consistent online A/B gains. Extensive experimental analyses further explain the gains achieved by AGR.

2 Problem Definition

For reference, the notation used throughout this paper is summarized in Table 7.

Generative Retrieval.

Given a request containing query qq and model-visible user context uvisu_{\mathrm{vis}}, generative retrieval aims to retrieve KK items from a corpus 𝒳\mathcal{X} by directly generating item identifiers. Each item x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} is represented by a hierarchical SID sequence 𝐬=[s1,…,sL]\mathbf{s}=[s_{1},\ldots,s_{L}], where si∈𝒮is_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{i} denotes the token at level ii and 𝐬⩽i=[s1,…,si]\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}=[s_{1},\ldots,s_{i}] denotes its prefix. The retriever generates the sequence autoregressively by modeling ℙθ​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i)\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}), and scores each prefix by accumulating token-level log-probabilities πθ​(𝐬⩽i)=∑j=1ilog⁡ℙθ​(sj∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽j−1)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}\left(s_{j}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant j-1}\right). During inference, a prefix trie Tr\mathrm{Tr} over valid SIDs constrains beam search to valid paths only. After LL decoding steps, the top-KK completed sequences are mapped to the corresponding items as results (Cao et al., 2021).

Feature Injection.

Beyond the visible request context qq and uvisu_{\mathrm{vis}}, practical GR systems often rely on heterogeneous auxiliary features, including long-term behaviors, user attributes, and other auxiliary signals stored in external services. We denote the candidate feature set as ℱ\mathcal{F}. Incorporating a subset ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} into decoding is referred to as feature injection, which falls into two categories:

  • •

    Static injection commits to a fixed subset ℱstatic⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{static}}\subseteq\mathcal{F} before decoding and reuses it at every step, so the same features influence the entire SID generation:

    πθ​(𝐬)=∑i=1Llog⁡ℙθ​(si∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i−1,ℱstatic).\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i-1},\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{static}}). (1)
  • •

    Dynamic injection selects a different subset at each step conditioned on the decoded prefix 𝐬x,<i\mathbf{s}_{x,<i}, allowing both the identity and the number of injected features to vary across decoding depths:

    πθ​(𝐬)=∑i=1Llog⁡ℙθ​(si∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i−1,ℱi), where ​ℱi⊆ℱ,ℱi=σ⁡(q,uvis,𝐬⩽i−1),\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i-1},\mathcal{F}_{i}),\quad\text{ where }\mathcal{F}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{F},\;\mathcal{F}_{i}=\sigma(q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i-1}), (2)

    where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is a prefix-aware feature selection policy. Static injection is recovered as the special case ℱi≡ℱstat\mathcal{F}_{i}\equiv\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{stat}} for all ii.

3 Limitations of Static Feature Injection

Having defined static and dynamic feature injection in GR, we now analyze why the static scheme adopted by most existing GR methods is insufficient (Rajput et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a). Motivated by the observed cost–gain imbalance of static injection at scale (Zhou et al., 2026), we compare a shared feature-free baseline with feature-specific static-injection models, where each model statically encodes one feature type into the input.

We begin with an empirical observation. As shown in Figure 1, increasing the amount of features injected statically, instantiated by user behavior sequences, leads to diminishing or even negative improvements for training, while increasing serving cost. This suggests that indiscriminate, static feature injection is neither consistently beneficial nor cost-efficient. Moving beyond static injection, dynamic injection raises two key challenges: when a feature should be incorporated across requests, and where in the SID hierarchy it should take effect.

For the first challenge, static injection assumes an injected feature is universally useful, rather than request-dependent. To diagnose this issue, we construct two test sets: feature-consistent set Fea., where the request and target item share the same feature value, and feature-conflicting set Comp., where their values differ. We measure the injection effect by the perplexity (Jelinek et al., 1977):

ΔPPL=PPLstatic−PPLw/o​feature,PPL=exp(−1L∑i=1Llogℙ(si∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i−1)).\Delta\mathrm{PPL}=\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{static}}-\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{w/o\ feature}},\quad\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\log\mathbb{P}(s_{i}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i-1})\right). (3)

As shown in Figure 2, the static injection model lowers PPL\mathrm{PPL} in Fea. set but raises it in Comp. set, confirming that feature utility is request-dependent. Therefore, efficient feature injection should be request-adaptive, using features only when beneficial.

For the second challenge, static injection exposes all decoding steps to the same features. However, RQ-based SIDs typically exhibit coarse-to-fine semantics, suggesting that different steps may require different features. To verify this, we identify, for each feature, the depth i∗i^{*} where injecting it would most improve next-token prediction (detailed in Section 4.2), and then measure whether static injection actually concentrates its effect at the depth i∗i^{*}. Concretely, we compare the golden-token probability ratio at each step:

ri=ℙstatic​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i)ℙw/o​feature​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i),r_{i}=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{static}}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{w/o\ feature}}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})}\,, (4)

where ℙstatic\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{static}} and ℙw/o​feature\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{w/o\ feature}} denote the golden-token probability produced by models with features statically injected into the model input and without any encoded features, respectively. As shown in Table 1, the probability ratio ri∗r_{i^{*}} is not consistently higher than at other levels. This confirms that static injection spreads its influence uniformly rather than concentrating it where the feature is most needed. Efficient feature injection therefore requires a level-adaptive mechanism that activates each feature only at the decoding depths where it is expected to be informative.

4 Methodology

To enable on-demand feature interaction, we propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR). Section 4.1 introduces the inference framework and tool implementation; Section 4.2 describes how data are constructed and used to operationalize this tool-augmented generative retrieval paradigm.

4.1 Agentic Generative Retrieval

AGR Framework.

To provide a flexible and extensible interface for feature interaction, we model tool calls and their results as tokens. Specifically, each tool token t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} triggers a function call ft​(q,u,𝐬⩽i)f_{t}(q,u,\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}), whose result is represented as an observation token ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}. By extending the vocabulary to 𝒱=𝒮∪𝒯∪𝒪\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{S}\cup\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{O}, the model naturally unifies SID generation and tool invocation into a single autoregressive process. As shown in Figure 3, given the request qq, user uvisu_{\mathrm{vis}}, decoded prefix 𝐬⩽i\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}, and prior observations, the model predicts either the next SID token si+1∈𝒮s_{i+1}\in\mathcal{S} or a tool token t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} (e.g. tIt_{\text{I}} or tGt_{\text{G}}). Specifically, tool tokens serve solely as decision triggers and are not fed back into the autoregressive context; only the returned observation token (e.g., oI{\color[rgb]{1,0.418,0.418}o_{\mathrm{I}}} or oG{\color[rgb]{0.4375,0.7539,0.7813}o_{\mathrm{G}}}) is injected, with distinct positional encodings to differentiate it from 𝒮\mathcal{S}. As a result, the decoder consumes a single token per step, yet still allowing observations to prune irrelevant branches during generation (e.g., the “Movie” branch in Figure 3). For more details, refer to Algorithm 2 and Example 1.

Tool Implementations.

Based on the type of observation returned, tools fall into two categories: structured feature tools, and sequential feature tools:

  1. (a)

    Structured feature tools return categorical values and can be directly encoded into a single learnable observation token — e.g., a game intent maps to oI:Game{\color[rgb]{1,0.418,0.418}o_{\mathrm{I}}\!:\!\mathrm{Game}}, a Beijing location to oL:Beijing{\color[rgb]{0.9609,0.6523,0.1367}o_{\mathrm{L}}\!:\!\mathrm{Beijing}}, and a high freshness requirement to oF:High{\color[rgb]{0.9688,0.1758,0.625}o_{\mathrm{F}}\!:\!\mathrm{High}}. Due to the hierarchical structure of RQ, items with similar features naturally share SID prefixes; for example, videos about games tend to cluster under the same prefixes (Rajput et al., 2023). Thus, these learnable observation tokens could serve as informative signals during decoding.

  2. (b)

    Sequential feature tools return user behavioral sequences (e.g., General Search Unit, GSU (Zhou et al., 2026)), which need to be encoded into a single observation token oG{\color[rgb]{0.4375,0.7539,0.7813}o_{\mathrm{G}}}. Various methods could accomplish this (Cao et al., 2026); we adopt two complementary approaches: Vote, a parameter-free approach that is efficient for training and inference, and Attn, which offers stronger user preference modeling capacity. As shown in Figure 4, Vote performs prefix matching: it selects items whose SID prefix matches the decoded one, then picks the most frequent next SID token (i.e., s3_7) via majority voting. Attn instead operates in the embedding space: it computes the accumulated residual representation of the decoded prefix (e.g., the sum of the embeddings of s1_1 and s2_3), retrieves the Top-EE (E=5E=5 for evaluation) most similar items from the sequence, and encodes their next SID token representations into a single embedding via multi-head attention. Unless otherwise stated, we use the Vote variant (Table 14).

4.2 Tool-augmented AGR Fine-tuning

Data Construction.

Having incorporated tool calls and observations into the token vocabulary (Section 4.1), we now describe how to construct training data that teaches the model to invoke tools during decoding. Concretely, for each positive sample x+x^{+} with target SIDs 𝐬+=[s1,…,sL]\mathbf{s}^{+}=[s_{1},\ldots,s_{L}], we augment the sequence by inserting a tool token tt at depth i∗i^{*} and its corresponding observation oto_{t} into the shifted input, so that the model predicts [s1,…,si∗,t,si∗+1,…,sL,eos][s_{1},\ldots,s_{i^{*}},t,s_{i^{*}+1},\ldots,s_{L},\text{eos}] from [bos,s1,…,si∗,ot,si∗+1,…,sL][\text{bos},s_{1},\ldots,s_{i^{*}},o_{t},s_{i^{*}+1},\ldots,s_{L}]. As outlined in Section 3, this construction requires answering two questions: when — which samples should be augmented with which tools, and where — at which decoding level 1⩽i∗<L1\leqslant i^{*}<L the tool should be invoked.

  • •

    “When” is a feature applicable? From the perspective of individual samples, tools are not universally applicable across all scenarios. Leveraging available supervised data, we identify when a tool is applicable and construct 𝒫⁡(x+)\mathcal{P}(x^{+}), the set of applicable tool-position pairs (t,i)(t,i) for each positive sample x+x^{+}.

    1. (a)

      For a structured feature tool tt, ot=ft​(q,u)o_{t}=f_{t}(q,u) extracts the feature from the request side (e.g., query and all user context) to produce observation oto_{t}, and gt​(x+)g_{t}(x^{+}) extracts the same feature from the positive sample x+x^{+}. To ensure both relevance and non-redundancy, we retain tt only when the two extractions agree, and the feature is not already explicit in the context:

      𝒫str(x+)={(t,i)∣ot=gt(x+)∧ot absent from model inputs, 1⩽i<L}.\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{str}}(x^{+})=\{(t,i)\mid o_{t}=g_{t}(x^{+})\land\ o_{t}\text{ absent from model inputs},\ 1\leqslant i<L\}. (5)
    2. (b)

      For a sequential feature tool tt, ot,i=ft​(q,u,𝐬⩽i+)o_{t,i}=f_{t}(q,u,\mathbf{s}^{+}_{\leqslant i}) derives its observation from user behavior sequences, while gt​(x+,𝐬⩽i+)=si+1+g_{t}(x^{+},\mathbf{s}^{+}_{\leqslant i})=s^{+}_{i+1} directly extracts the golden next SID. We instantiate ftf_{t} with the Vote variant fvotef_{\mathrm{vote}}. Similarly, we retain tt only when the two extractions agree:

      𝒫seq(x+)={(t,i)∣ot,i=si+1+, 1⩽i<L}.\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{seq}}(x^{+})=\left\{(t,i)\mid o_{t,i}=s^{+}_{i+1},\ 1\leqslant i<L\right\}. (6)

      To make the model robust to ineffective tool calls, we also sample incorrect predictions, maintaining a voting hit rate of τ\tau to control the hit-to-miss ratio.

  • •

    “Where” to insert the feature? Having identified the samples amenable to tool insertion, we now determine the optimal depth i∗i^{*} to insert tools. The key intuition is that a feature should be injected at the depth where it best disambiguates the next SID token. We formalize this via ρi\rho_{i}, which reflects how discriminative the feature is at that prefix. The depth where ρ\rho changes most sharply is selected as the most valuable position for feature injection:

    it∗​(x+)=arg​maxi⁡[ρi+1​(ot)−ρi​(ot)]s.t.​(t,i)∈𝒫⁡(x+),i_{t}^{*}(x^{+})=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\end{subarray}}\left[\rho_{i+1}(o_{t})-\rho_{i}(o_{t})\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\ (t,i)\in\mathcal{P}(x^{+}), (7)

    where 𝒫=𝒫str\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{str}} for structured feature tools and 𝒫=𝒫seq\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{seq}} for sequential feature tools. We define ρi\rho_{i} for each tool type as follows:

    1. (a)

      For a structured feature tool, the observation is a discrete attribute of items. To identify where injecting this feature narrows the candidate set most, therefore best disambiguates the next SID token, we compute the log-proportion of items under prefix 𝐬⩽i+\mathbf{s}^{+}_{\leqslant i} that share the same attribute value over the corpus 𝒳\mathcal{X}:

      ρi​(ot)=log⁡ℙx′∼𝒳​(gt​(x′)=ot∣𝐬⩽i+).\displaystyle\rho_{i}(o_{t})=\log\mathbb{P}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{X}}\left(g_{t}(x^{\prime})=o_{t}\mid\mathbf{s}^{+}_{\leqslant i}\right). (8)

      The sharpest increase in ρi\rho_{i} identifies the depth where the feature becomes most discriminative, therefore provides the strongest signal for predicting the next SID.

    2. (b)

      For a sequential feature tool, the observation is the next SID token voted from behavior sequences. To measure where this observation narrows the candidate set most, we compute the log-proportion of items under prefix 𝐬⩽i+\mathbf{s}^{+}_{\leqslant i} that share the same next token over 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}:

      ρi​(ot,i)=log⁡ℙx′∼𝒟train​(gt​(x′,𝐬⩽i′)=ot,i∣𝐬⩽i+).\displaystyle\rho_{i}(o_{t,i})=\log\mathbb{P}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\left(g_{t}(x^{\prime},\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{\leqslant i})=o_{t,i}\mid\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}^{+}\right). (9)

      By Theorem 3, maximizing the increase in ρi\rho_{i} is equivalent to maximizing the model’s prediction gain (i.e., ri=ℙθ/ℙw/o featuresr_{i}=\mathbb{P}_{\theta}/\mathbb{P}_{\text{w/o features}}, analogous to Eq. 4); both are further equivalent to minimizing ρi\rho_{i} itself. Accordingly, for sequential feature placement, we typically adopt the equivalent criterion i∗=arg⁡mini​ρi​(ot,i)i^{*}=\arg\min_{i}\rho_{i}(o_{t,i}). Intuitively, a lower ρi\rho_{i} indicates that the golden SID is rarer among items sharing the same prefix, making the observation more informative for identifying the user’s fine-grained or niche preferences.

    The “when” and “where” decisions are illustrated in Example 2.

Two-Stage Training.

To decouple semantic learning from tool integration for better extensibility, AGR training consists of two stages. The first stage leverages GR (SID-only) data to learn SID generation following traditional GR methods (Chen et al., 2025c). The second stage then introduces AGR data, where the model learns to integrate tool calls into generation. The loss now covers both SID tokens and tool tokens. In practice, since tool tokens are unseen during the first stage, their token-level losses are initially much higher than those of SID tokens, risking destabilization of already-learned representations. To mitigate this imbalance, we scale the loss of each tool token by a factor αk\alpha_{k} that adapts per training step. Formally, let 𝐯out​(x)=[v1,…,v|𝐯out|]\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}}(x)=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{|\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}}|}] denote the decoder output sequence for the given sample xx. For mini-batch ℬk\mathcal{B}_{k} at step kk, we measure the prediction difficulty gap between tool and SID tokens: βk=𝔼(x,j)∼ℬk​[log⁡ℙθ​(vj∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽j−1)∣vj∉𝒯]𝔼(x,j)∼ℬk​[log⁡ℙθ​(vj∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽j−1)∣vj∈𝒯]\beta_{k}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{(x,j)\sim\mathcal{B}_{k}}[\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(v_{j}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant j-1})\mid v_{j}\notin\mathcal{T}]}{\mathbb{E}_{(x,j)\sim\mathcal{B}_{k}}[\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(v_{j}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant j-1})\mid v_{j}\in\mathcal{T}]} and clip it to [αmin\alpha_{\min}, αmax\alpha_{\max}] for stability αk=𝟏[vj∈𝒯]⋅clip(βk,αmin,αmax)+𝟏[vj∉𝒯].\alpha_{k}=\mathbf{1}[v_{j}\in\mathcal{T}]\cdot\operatorname{clip}(\beta_{k},\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max})+\mathbf{1}[v_{j}\notin\mathcal{T}]. The final objective is then delivered as:

ℒAGR=−1|ℬk|∑x∈Bk1|𝐯out|∑j=1|𝐯out|αk⋅logℙθ(vj∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽j−1).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AGR}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{k}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{\mathcal{}}{B}_{k}}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}}|}\alpha_{k}\cdot\log\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(v_{j}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant j-1}). (10)

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate AGR on four datasets: Industry, Qilin, JDSearch, and KuaiSAR (large). Industry is derived from real-world user behavior logs collected from Kuaishou Search, with approximately 300 million records per day; we use June 14–20 for the first training stage, June 21–22 for the second training stage, and June 23 for testing. Qilin is a multimodal retrieval benchmark with app-level user sessions (Chen et al., 2025b); JDSearch focuses on personalized product-search benchmark with real queries and user–item interactions (Liu et al., 2023); and KuaiSAR provides a unified search-and-recommendation benchmark (Sun et al., 2023b). Further details are provided in Table 8.

AGR Implementations.

We adopt a 12-layer encoder-decoder BART (Lewis et al., 2020) as the backbone (≈\approx 574M parameters, including embeddings for approximately 19,000 predefined SID codewords) and construct hierarchical SIDs via RQ-KMeans (Rajput et al., 2023). Dataset-specific SID configurations and tool sets are listed in Table 9; inference follows Algorithm 2. On the large-scale Industry dataset, we train the model sequentially in two stages, with each stage running for one epoch over its corresponding aggregated training data. For the smaller public datasets, we fine-tune with each method for 10 epochs until convergence. For fair comparison, within each dataset, all methods share the same text-pretrained backbone, SID codebooks, training data, learning rate, and hardware configuration. Additional details are provided in Appendix A.

Evaluation Metrics.

We adopt Recall@KK and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@KK) with K∈{32,50,64}K\in\{32,50,64\} (K=50K=50 for online A/B test). Given NN test requests, for ii-th query, let 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} denote the ground-truth item set, ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} the top-KK retrieved items, and rir_{i} the rank of the first ground-truth item (ri=∞r_{i}=\infty if none appears in the top-KK). Formally, we have:

Recall​@⁡K=1N​∑i=1N|𝒢i∩ℛi||𝒢i|andMRR​@⁡K=1N​∑i=1N𝕀[ri⩽K]ri.\operatorname{Recall@}K=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|\mathcal{G}_{i}\cap\mathcal{R}_{i}|}{|\mathcal{G}_{i}|}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{MRR@}K=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\mathbb{I}[r_{i}\leqslant K]}{r_{i}}. (11)

5.2 Main Results

As shown in Table 2, AGR consistently outperforms all baselines across all datasets and evaluation metrics. We compare AGR with five generative retrieval baselines: TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023) for standard GR baseline; TIGER Distill Teacher, which first trains a teacher model with up to 400 GSU tokens (Table 4) and then distills its predictions into TIGER using an auxiliary distillation loss with a weight of 0.10.1; UniSearch (Chen et al., 2025c) for unified short-video retrieval; and GLASS (Cao et al., 2026) and GEMs (Zhou et al., 2026) for long-history modeling. AGR achieves the best Recall and MRR at all cutoffs, with relative improvements over TIGER ranging from 6.4% to 14.0% in Recall and from 5.2% to 19.7% in MRR. Its advantages over TIGER Distill Teacher and UniSearch demonstrate the benefit of dynamically acquiring request-specific evidence during decoding, a capability absent from these methods. Its advantages over GLASS and GEMs further demonstrate that adaptive tool integration exploits long-term behavioral features more effectively than direct sequence modeling.

5.3 Ablation Study

Our ablation and analysis primarily focus on the Industry dataset, as it supports more diverse tool construction than existing public benchmarks. Additional ablations and analyses are in Section C.

Adaptive feature injection outperforms predetermined strategies.

A defining principle of AGR is that feature injection should be driven by the model’s generation state rather than predetermined. We ablate this across four strategies over a feature set including intent, location, freshness and GSU sequence. Static feature injection feeds all features into the encoder without selection or weighting. Query-guided gating uses a lightweight MLP, whose parameter count is substantially smaller (≈\approx4,100 parameters) than that of the backbone, to learn query-dependent feature weights. Fixed-position tool injection retrieves features via tool calls, but at a predetermined position. AGR uses the same tool-call mechanism but injects adaptively. As shown in Table 3, query-guided gating and fixed-position injection both outperform static injection, yet AGR achieves the best Recall@50, confirming the effectiveness of adaptive injection.

Sequential feature tools match long sequence encoding at a fraction of the cost.

Tool-based retrieval compresses sequential features into discrete observations to keep serving cost manageable. We quantify this trade-off by comparing AGR with directly appending up to 400 GSU tokens to the input. As shown in Table 4, direct encoding improves Recall@50 from 0.2863 to 0.3241, but at steep cost: training time rises from 1.163 to 10.794 seconds per step, and serving cost rises from 2.38 to 8.33 GPUs per 1K requests. In contrast, AGR achieves comparable Recall@50 of 0.3237, while reducing training time and serving cost by 81.8% and 42.9%. Although AGR roughly doubles the serving cost over the no-feature baseline, it remains far more efficient than direct encoding.

5.4 Experimental Analysis

AGR recovers baseline failures through selective, precise tool usage.

To trace the source of AGR’s gains, we partition 10,000 Industry test instances into four quadrants by comparing AGR against the tool-free baseline: Comfort (both hit), Ambiguity (both miss), Recovery (only AGR hits), and Error (only baseline hits). As shown in Table 5, Recovery accounts for 14.1% of instances versus 7.9% for Error, yielding a net improvement of +6.2pp in Recall@50. Notably, tool invocation is heavily concentrated in Recovery, where the tool-call rate reaches 44.8%, far above the 20.6% overall average. Within Recovery, we further compare tool-invoking and no-tool beams among the most confident top-10 beams for each query: tool-invoking beams achieve a 15.1% hit rate versus 3.7% for no-tool beams (4.1×4.1\times), and every tool type outperforms the no-tool beams. These findings confirm that AGR selectively invokes tools on queries the baseline fails, and that tool-assisted beams are substantially more likely to retrieve the correct item.

AGR yields disproportionately larger gains where features matter most.

To examine whether AGR’s improvements are tied to genuine feature relevance, we partition the data into Fea. and Comp. subsets based on whether the target item is characterized by the corresponding feature (Section 3). As shown in Figure 5(a), AGR achieves more than twice the recall gain on Fea. compared to Comp., confirming that its improvements concentrate on feature-dependent queries rather than arising from uniform score shifts.

AGR injects evidence at the right moment, avoiding the degradation caused by ill-timed feature injection.

To examine whether AGR resolves the challenge of “when” in static injection, we report Δ​PPL=PPLAGR−PPLw/o​feature\Delta\mathrm{PPL}=\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{AGR}}-\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{w/o\ feature}} (analogous to Eq. 3) on the Fea. and Comp. set. As shown in Figure 2, static injection lowers PPL on Fea. but raises it on Comp., exposing its inability to sense when feature injection is actually needed. AGR, by contrast, yields negative Δ​PPL\Delta\mathrm{PPL} on both sets (Figure 5(b)), with a consistently larger reduction on Fea., confirming that it activates tool calls only when evidence is beneficial and withholds them otherwise.

AGR concentrates feature signals at the most informative positions rather than spreading them indiscriminately.

To examine whether AGR resolves the challenge of “where” in static injection, we let i∗=arg​maxi⁡Δ​ρii^{*}=\argmax_{i}\Delta\rho_{i} denote the SID level with the largest change in feature concentration and measure the golden-token probability ratio (Eq. 4) at i∗i^{*} relative to other levels. As shown in Figure 5(c), static injection produces nearly the same ratio at i∗i^{*} and elsewhere, whereas AGR consistently yields a larger ratio at i∗i^{*} for every feature, with the contrast strongest for Location (1.116 vs. 1.012) and Freshness (1.218 vs. 1.063), confirming that AGR allocates feature influence precisely where it carries the most discriminative power.

5.5 Online A/B Test

We deploy AGR in our production search system with an average serving latency of 35ms, well within our online budget. We then conduct a live experiment consisting of a 7-day A/A test followed by a 7-day A/B test, with the production baseline and AGR each serving 10% of randomly sampled user traffic. As shown in Table 6, AGR yields consistent gains along three axes of user experience. Relevance, defined as the fraction of PVs (i.e., search requests) whose top-4 results are strongly relevant to the query, improves by +0.205%, indicating that AGR retrieves more query-relevant items. Query reformulation rate drops by -0.690%, showing that users are more often satisfied on the first query and no longer need to rephrase it. Finally, search penetration rate, defined as the fraction of users who engage with search, rises by +0.06%. As an upstream user-behavior metric that AGR does not optimize directly, its improvement suggests that better single-query experience propagates into higher willingness to use search.

6 Limitations and Future Work

AGR interleaves tool invocation with SID generation, but has three limitations. First, its training data are constructed using predefined rules rather than learned policies; future work could apply agentic reinforcement learning to optimize tool use under the sparse rewards common in search and recommendation. Second, the current tool ecosystem is limited and should be extended to more tools and retrieval domains. Third, trajectories are constructed along golden SID prefixes using target-side agreement, creating a gap from free-running inference. Optimizing and evaluating tool decisions under model-generated prefixes is therefore an important future direction.

7 Conclusion

We presented Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), a tool-augmented paradigm that selectively acquires and incorporates heterogeneous features during hierarchical SID generation. AGR determines when, and where features should be introduced based on the request and decoded SID prefix. We train this capability using tool-augmented data constructed from feature applicability and discriminability. Evaluations on an industrial dataset and public benchmarks, together with an online A/B test, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of AGR, highlighting tool-augmented generation as a promising direction for large-scale generative retrieval.

Appendix A AGR Implementations

This section provides further implementation details of AGR. For datasets with textual features (Industry and Qilin (Chen et al., 2025b)), we adopt Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024) as a parameter-shared dual-encoder model and train it with Query-to-Item (Q2I) supervision. For anonymous datasets (JDSearch (Liu et al., 2023) and KuaiSAR (Sun et al., 2023b)), we instead use TwinBERT (Lu et al., 2020) to obtain item embeddings. We then apply hierarchical RQ-KMeans to construct their Semantic ID (SID) codebooks. Specifically, for the Industry dataset, which contains billions of recall samples, we use codebook sizes of (8192,4096,2048,2048,2048)(8192,4096,2048,2048,2048), whereas for the comparatively smaller public datasets, we use (512,256,128)(512,256,128). We next describe the implementation of AGR in terms of tools, model architecture, inference, training-data construction, and training procedure.

A.1 Datasets and Settings

Table 8 shows the details of the used datasets, Table 9 summarizes the two types of tools and their dataset-specific implementations, and Table 10 summarizes the training and inference settings.

A.2 Tool Implementations

For structured feature tools, each categorical value is represented by a learnable observation embedding, initialized by mean-pooling the pretrained embeddings of the text tokens corresponding to its feature value. For sequential feature tools, historical GSU items are stored with their hierarchical SIDs. The Attn variant uses E=5E=5 retrieved GSU items and an 8-head attention module to aggregate their successor-SID representations. Observation tokens use absolute positional embeddings distinct from those of autoregressive SID tokens, such that an injected observation conditions the next prediction without advancing the SID decoding depth.

A.3 Model Inference

Inference interface and adaptive interaction.

We instantiate AGR with BART, although the method only requires an autoregressive interface and also supports decoder-only backbones such as Qwen. As Figure 3 illustrates, its input and output spaces are asymmetric: the output contains generated SIDs and tool-call decisions, whereas the decoder input contains SIDs and externally returned observations. A generated SID is fed back autoregressively; a generated tool token instead triggers external execution, and the returned observation is fed into the next decoding step. This interface represents every tool call and observation with one decoding position and uses distinct positional encodings to separate observations from SID decisions. The quota MM is maintained separately for every beam-decoding path. A quota of MM calls therefore adds at most MM decoding steps to each path, so an LL-token SID requires at most L+M+1L+M+1 steps including eos. Tool calls are neither fixed to predetermined positions nor required to alternate with SIDs. At each incomplete depth, the model may select either a valid SID successor or an available tool. The method described in Section 4.2 determines an admissible position at which to invoke each tool so as to maximize the discriminability of the feature. Theorem 3 further characterizes the position at which the feature is most informative w.r.t. sequential features.

Example 1 (AGR Workflow).

Figure 3 illustrates how AGR interleaves SID generation with feature acquisition for the query “Fighting Zombies”. After the first SID token is generated, the prefix may lead to either the movie or game branch, making the next prediction uncertain. The model therefore emits the intent-tool token tIt_{\text{I}} and receives the game-intent observation oI:Game{\color[rgb]{1,0.418,0.418}o_{\mathrm{I}}\!:\!\mathrm{Game}}, which steers decoding toward games while suppressing irrelevant movie candidates. Further along the game branch, query relevance alone cannot distinguish among candidates such as Minecraft and Plants vs. Zombies. The model thus emits the GSU-tool token tGt_{\text{G}} to acquire user preferences from historical behaviors. As shown in Figure 4, Vote retains items whose SIDs exactly match the decoded prefix (A, B, and D) and returns the most frequent successor SID, s3_7, indicating a preference for Minecraft. In contrast, Attn exploits the residual clustering structure of SIDs: summing the embeddings of the decoded SID tokens reconstructs the prefix representation at the current decoding depth. It then retrieves the Top-EE historical behaviors whose item representations are closest to this reconstructed prefix representation, thereby including approximate matches such as C, and aggregates their successor SIDs via lightweight multi-head attention. Both implementations provide fine-grained preference signals that steer decoding toward the user’s preferred Minecraft branch while suppressing irrelevant candidates.

Beam search.

The blue-gray lines in Algorithm 2 highlight the core changes relative to the normal trie-based beam search in Algorithm 1. Both algorithms maintain candidates (𝐯in,𝐯out,z)(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{in}},\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}},z) and expand trie-valid SID successors. Their main differences are: First, conventional decoding uses the fixed L+1L+1 horizon (Algorithm 1, line 4), whereas AGR reserves MM additional steps and exposes tool tokens only while quota remains (Algorithm 2, line 4 and line 20). Second, the conventional update appends every predicted token to both sequences (Algorithm 1, line 9); AGR instead appends a tool token only to 𝐯out\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}} and its external observation only to 𝐯in\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{in}}, while retaining the conventional update for SIDs (Algorithm 2, lines 10). Third, conventional beam search ranks the current fixed-length expansions by zz (Algorithm 1, line 10); AGR jointly compares active and completed variable-length paths using the length-normalized score z/|𝐯out|z/|\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{out}}| (Algorithm 2, lines 13). Finally, the conventional return removes only eos (Algorithm 1, line 11), whereas AGR additionally removes tool tokens to recover the same SID-only output space (Algorithm 2, line 15).

A.4 Data Construction and Training

Training-data construction.

Section 4.2 presents the overall procedure for constructing tool-augmented supervision. When multiple tools are simultaneously applicable under a limited tool quota MM, we prioritize tools with higher coverage in the training data. Eq. 8 and Eq. 9 use 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, respectively, to determine tool insertion positions: the former enables the model, while learning the empirical distribution from 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, to retrieve the true distribution of the required structural features along SID in 𝒳\mathcal{X} through tool calls, while the latter intends to inject less popular preferences through target items in 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}. Example 2 provides a complete worked example illustrating the considerations for structured feature tools, including when each tool is applicable and where its observation should be inserted.

Example 2 (Tool-augmented Training Data Construction).

Follow the query “Fighting Zombies” in Example 1, Figure 6 shows the golden SID path “s1_1→s2_1→s3_2→…\text{s1\_1}\rightarrow\text{s2\_1}\rightarrow\text{s3\_2}\rightarrow\ldots” of the positive item. Each path contains 10 items. The numbers of items with the intent oI:Gameo_{\mathrm{I}}\!:\!\mathrm{Game} under s3_1, s3_2, s3_3, and s3_4 are respectively 88, 99, 22, and 11. Therefore, along the golden path, the numbers of Game items are 20/4020/40 under s1_1, 17/2017/20 under s2_1, and 9/109/10 under s3_2.

    “When” is a tool applicable? Suppose the tool returns ot=oI:Gameo_{t}={\color[rgb]{1,0.418,0.418}o_{\mathrm{I}}\!:\!\mathrm{Game}}. It can be invoked because the query intent matches the intent of the positive item and the intent is absent from the keyword “Fighting Zombies” and user features.

The concentrations along the golden path are ρi​(ot)=log⁡(20/40)\rho_{i}(o_{t})=\log(20/40) under s1_1, ρi+1​(ot)=log⁡(17/20)\rho_{i+1}(o_{t})=\log(17/20) under s2_1, and ρi+2​(ot)=log⁡(9/10)\rho_{i+2}(o_{t})=\log(9/10) under s3_2. The corresponding gains are log⁡(17/20)−log⁡(20/40)=log⁡(1.7)\log(17/20)-\log(20/40)=\log(1.7) and log⁡(9/10)−log⁡(17/20)=log⁡(1.06)\log(9/10)-\log(17/20)=\log(1.06). Because the first gain is larger, the tool is invoked after s1_1, before generating s2_1.

The example above illustrates how to construct tool-augmented training data. Each tool’s insertion depth maximizes the increase of discriminability in Eq. 7. The selected tool token is inserted into the target output, while its observation appears only at the corresponding position in the shifted decoder input. During inference, each beam path independently decides at which decoding depth to invoke a tool, subject to its own per-path call quota.

Appendix B Interpretive Analysis

B.1 An Interpretive View of Dynamic Feature Interaction

This section provides an interpretive account of dynamic feature interaction. It is not intended as a general performance guarantee for AGR. Instead, it explains a simple design intuition: as the decoded SID prefix becomes more fine-grained, the information that is useful for predicting the next SID token may also change.

Theorem 1 (Contextual Incremental Information).

A feature observation oto_{t} is useful w.r.t. model ℙθ\mathbb{P}_{\theta} only if it adds information beyond the current context (i.e., q,uvisq,u_{\mathrm{vis}} and 𝐬⩽i\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}).

Proof.

Consider the conditional mutual information at the current context by definition:

Iθ(si+1;ot∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i)\displaystyle I_{\theta}(s_{i+1};o_{t}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})
=𝔼⁡[𝔻KL​(ℙθ​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i,ot)∥ℙθ​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i))].\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},o_{t})\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})\right)\right]. (12)

If this quantity is zero, the nonnegativity of the KL divergence implies that

ℙθ​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i,ot)=ℙθ​(si+1∣q,uvis,𝐬⩽i)almost surely.\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},o_{t})=\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\mid q,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})\quad\text{almost surely}. (13)

Hence, oto_{t} provides no additional predictive information for the next SID token at the current context (i.e., q,uvis,𝐬⩽iq,u_{\mathrm{vis}},\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}). The contrapositive proves the theorem. ∎

Although conditional mutual information is nonnegative in expectation, the predictive gain of a realized observation can vary across contexts. This consideration is particularly important in industrial search and recommendation systems, where numerous features are available to characterize complex and evolving user preferences, yet generative retrieval models can incorporate only limited additional information during decoding because of efficiency and scalability constraints. Feature injection must therefore be selective, retaining observations that improve prediction at the current prefix while avoiding those that provide no gain or reduce the probability of the correct next SID token. Our method implements this context-dependent selection through tool invocation and observation injection (Section 4); next, we analyze this mechanism through experiments on tool selection and invocation.

Generative Retrieval Knapsack Problem (GR-KP).

In AGR, the feature selection is implemented through tool interaction. Given the current context, predicting a tool token t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} invokes its associated function ftf_{t} and returns an observation ot=ft​(q,u,𝐬⩽i)o_{t}=f_{t}(q,u,\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}). The returned observation token is then injected into the decoder to influence subsequence prediction. We formulate this feature injection as a Generative Retrieval Knapsack Problem (GR-KP). At context q,uvisq,u_{\mathrm{vis}} and 𝐬⩽i\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}, invoking tool tt incurs cost ct>0c_{t}>0 and yields context-dependent value vt​(𝐬⩽i)v_{t}(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}), which summarizes the contribution of its returned observation to decoding process. Let γt∈[0,1]\gamma_{t}\in[0,1] denote the allocation assigned to each tool tt. Under a finite model capacity CθC_{\theta}, the feasible allocation set Γ\Gamma and its value VV are

Γ={𝜸=(γt)t∈𝒯| 0⩽γt⩽1,∑t∈𝒯ctγt⩽Cθ},V(𝐬⩽i,𝜸)=∑t∈𝒯γtvt(𝐬⩽i).\Gamma=\left\{\bm{\gamma}=(\gamma_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\,\middle|\,0\leqslant\gamma_{t}\leqslant 1,\ \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}c_{t}\gamma_{t}\leqslant C_{\theta}\right\},\quad V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma})=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\gamma_{t}v_{t}(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}). (14)

Here, fractional allocation provides a compact estimator of the benefit of feature selection in a capacity-limited generative model. As discussed in Section 3, static injection assigns a single allocation 𝜸\bm{\gamma} shared across all prefixes, whereas dynamic injection assigns a separate allocation 𝜸i\bm{\gamma}_{i} to the corresponding prefix 𝐬⩽i\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}. Thus, the optimal expected cumulative utility under static and dynamic injection are

𝒥static=max𝜸∈Γ⁡𝔼⁡[∑iV⁡(𝐬⩽i,𝜸)],𝒥dynamic=𝔼⁡[∑imax𝜸i∈Γ⁡V⁡(𝐬⩽i,𝜸i)].\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{static}}=\max_{\bm{\gamma}\in\Gamma}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma})\right],\qquad\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}\max_{\bm{\gamma}_{i}\in\Gamma}V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma}_{i})\right]. (15)
Theorem 2 (Dynamic Injection is Better).

When the usefulness of tool-derived features depends on the prefix 𝐬⩽i\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}, dynamic injection is at least as effective as static injection, i.e., 𝒥dynamic≥𝒥static.\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\geq\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{static}}.

Proof.

Recall that static injection selects one allocation 𝜸∈Γ\bm{\gamma}\in\Gamma and uses it for every prefix: 𝒥static=max𝜸∈Γ⁡𝔼⁡[∑iV⁡(𝐬⩽i,𝜸)].\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{static}}=\max_{\bm{\gamma}\in\Gamma}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i}V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma})\right]. A dynamic injection is allowed to choose an allocation 𝜸i​(𝐬⩽i)∈Γ\bm{\gamma}_{i}(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})\in\Gamma after observing the current prefix. In particular, it can imitate any static policy by setting 𝜸i​(𝐬⩽i)=𝜸,for all ​𝐬⩽i.\bm{\gamma}_{i}(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i})=\bm{\gamma},\text{for all }\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i}. Thus, every static allocation is feasible for the dynamic injection, and therefore

𝒥dynamic=𝔼⁡[∑imax𝜸i∈Γ⁡V⁡(𝐬⩽i,𝜸i)]≥maxγ∈Γ⁡𝔼⁡[∑iV⁡(𝐬⩽i,𝜸)]=𝒥static.\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i}\max_{\bm{\gamma}_{i}\in\Gamma}V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma}_{i})\right]\geq\max_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i}V(\mathbf{s}_{\leqslant i},\bm{\gamma})\right]=\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{static}}. (16)

∎

This indicates that dynamic injection is a more dynamic and superior feature selection planning compared to static injection.

Appendix C Further Ablation study and Analysis

Observations contribute genuine feature information, not merely extra decoding steps.

To verify that performance gains stem from the specific feature information carried by tool observations rather than from additional reasoning tokens, we replace per-observation tokens with a single shared learnable token, equivalent to a late-reasoning approach (AGR w/ shared observations). As shown in Table 11, this reasoning variant already outperforms the Baseline, confirming that extra decoding steps alone provide a non-trivial benefit. Yet AGR with distinct observation tokens achieves further gains, demonstrating that the observation tokens carry substantive feature information beyond what additional steps can provide.

Structured feature tools outperform the direct encoding approach.

In the AGR model, structured feature tools are incorporated into the decoding process through a token, depending on whether the relevant information is required at the current decoding step. An intuitive alternative is to directly integrate this information into the model’s encoding to evaluate its potential benefits. As shown in Table 12, directly encoding the relevant information improves performance compared to the baseline (from 0.2863 to 0.3013). However, the encoding strategy employed by AGR achieves even better results, with a score of 0.3137. This demonstrates that introducing relevant information on demand during the decoding process reduces the inclusion of noisy information, thereby enabling more efficient information encoding.

AGR’s gains persist across backbone architectures and model scales.

To examine the effects of backbone architecture and model scale, we evaluate UniSearch and AGR using BART (Lewis et al., 2020) and Qwen3 backbones with 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters (Yang et al., 2025). As shown in Table 13, Qwen3-0.6B outperforms the similarly sized BART backbone, suggesting that stronger pretrained language modeling provides benefits beyond parameter count alone. Scaling Qwen3 generally improves performance, with the 4B backbone achieving the best overall results. More importantly, AGR consistently outperforms UniSearch under every matched backbone, demonstrating that its improvements cannot be attributed solely to model capacity. These results confirm that backbone scaling and AGR provide complementary gains: larger pretrained models offer a stronger foundation, while explicit feature selection and targeted injection further improve SID generation across architectures and scales.

The impact of fusion modes in sequential feature tools: attention-based fusion is most accurate; voting is the practical default.

As discussed in Section 4.1, we implement two fusion modes for sequential feature tools (Vote and Attn) and introduce Mean as an additional baseline. Mean filters GSUs by prefix matching and averages their embeddings uniformly, discarding candidate importance variations; as expected, it yields the weakest results (Table 14). Attn achieves the best performance by relaxing strict prefix matching and learning adaptive fusion weights, confirming that candidate importance is both heterogeneous and learnable. Nevertheless, since Vote reaches comparable performance at substantially lower deployment cost, we adopt it as the default throughout this paper.

Tool loss rescaling prevents newly introduced tool tokens from disrupting SID semantics.

Stage-II training introduces tool tokens on top of the SID generation ability learned in Stage-I, creating a scale mismatch between the pretrained SID objective and the newly added tool objective. To test whether this mismatch matters, we compare training with and without the batch-wise rescaling coefficient αk\alpha_{k} in Eq. 10. As shown in Figure 7(a), rescaling consistently improves Recall@1, while Figure 7(b) shows a clear early-stage gap between SID- and tool-token loss magnitudes. This confirms that optimizing tool tokens at their raw scale can disturb the pretrained SID semantics, whereas αk\alpha_{k} calibrates the two objectives and enables stable tool-enhanced semantic learning.

Appendix D Related Works

Generative retrieval and semantic identifiers.

Distinct from traditional discriminative retrieval (Xie et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2024), generative retrieval reformulates retrieval as conditional sequence generation over discrete identifiers (Chen et al., 2025c; Tay et al., 2022). Early work focused on document retrieval, where DSI stores query–document associations in model parameters (Tay et al., 2022), NCI introduces structured identifiers and prefix-aware decoding (Wang et al., 2022), and SEAL uses document-derived textual access paths (Bevilacqua et al., 2022). These studies established that the identifier space is learnable and that errors at different decoding positions have different retrieval consequences (Sun et al., 2023a; Zeng et al., 2024). Generative recommendation extends this idea to multi-token item semantic identifiers (SIDs). TIGER quantizes item representations with RQ-VAE and generates hierarchical SIDs (Rajput et al., 2023), making coarse-to-fine constrained decoding a standard formulation. Subsequent work shows that SID quality depends on semantic consistency, discrimination, codebook utilization, and tree balance (Ju et al., 2026), while autoregressive SID trees may also restrict ranking expressiveness (Hou et al., 2026). AGR builds on this SID-based generative retrieval paradigm, but shifts the focus from how identifiers are constructed to how external evidence should interact with SID generation.

Feature conditioning in generative retrieval.

Real-world GR systems rely on heterogeneous auxiliary information, including user profiles, behavioral histories, scenario context, freshness signals, and intent features. Existing methods usually incorporate such information before decoding or through a fixed injection pattern (Wang et al., 2025). DiffusionGS performs query-conditioned denoising over candidate items (Li et al., 2026b); DualGR separates long- and short-term user interests (Yi et al., 2026); GLASS retrieves user histories conditioned on coarse SIDs (Cao et al., 2026); and OneReason partitions behavioral histories into temporal streams (Team et al., 2026). These methods show that request-aware evidence selection is important, and they move beyond globally encoding all context indiscriminately. However, their injection mechanisms are still largely predetermined: evidence is selected before generation, kept fixed after a coarse decision, or injected at predefined network locations. They do not formulate feature acquisition itself as an explicit decoding-time action. AGR differs by expanding the generative action space with tool tokens, allowing the model to decide whether a feature is needed, which feature to acquire, and where in the SID hierarchy the acquired evidence should affect subsequent generation.

Industrial GR systems and optimization.

Industrial systems pursue GR for unification, cross-domain reuse, and serving efficiency. UniSearch jointly trains generators and encoders for video and live search (Chen et al., 2025c); OneSearch develops task-aware SID construction for e-commerce (Chen et al., 2025a); IntSR shares models across search and recommendation (Yan et al., 2025); OneRec unifies retrieval and ranking (Deng et al., 2025); and OneMall extends GR across multiple scenarios (Zhang et al., 2026b). Complementary work improves SID construction, collision control, and long-term maintenance (Wang et al., 2026c; Fu et al., 2026b; Baikalov et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026), and generative interfaces have also been extended to reranking and query recommendation (Yang et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2025). Beyond maximum-likelihood training, preference-oriented methods align GR with ranking quality or business value: UniSearch uses ranking signals (Chen et al., 2025c), while related methods apply preference optimization to e-commerce (Li et al., 2024), adapt DPO to hierarchical SIDs (Chen et al., 2026b), use listwise optimization (Fu et al., 2026a), generative flow networks (Wang et al., 2026a), token-level signals (Lin et al., 2026), iterative preference construction (Deng et al., 2025), page-wise supervision (Zou et al., 2026), and list-level value optimization (Xue et al., 2026). Efficiency methods accelerate decoding through draft verification (Wang et al., 2026b), process reward models (Guo et al., 2026), and load-aware computation (Xue et al., 2026). These efforts optimize different components of large-scale GR pipelines, whereas AGR targets a complementary bottleneck: avoiding noisy and expensive static feature injection by acquiring useful features on demand during decoding.

Reasoning and agentic retrieval.

Recent work introduces intermediate reasoning to improve intent understanding in search and recommendation. OneSearch-V2 constructs keyword-based chains of thought (Chen et al., 2026a); OneRec-Think interleaves textual reasoning with generation (Liu et al., 2025); SCoTER transfers structured reasoning from LLMs (Jiang et al., 2025); DiffuReason combines latent thinking with diffusion refinement (Jiang et al., 2026); and OneReason organizes recommendation around perception and cognition (Team et al., 2026). Agentic recommendation further allows models to actively acquire external evidence. KP-Agent combines LLM agents with domain tools (Long et al., 2025), and ChainRec learns to route and terminate tool chains (Li et al., 2026a). However, general-purpose LLM planning typically introduces sequential inference, external orchestration, and tool-chain latency, which are difficult to accommodate in latency-constrained retrieval. Unlike these agentic recommenders, AGR treats feature access as a lightweight action inside native constrained SID decoding. Tool invocation is not a separate planning loop, but an interleaved part of beam search that directly reshapes the probability distribution over subsequent SID tokens.
